label: Spectral Theory
notes: Open the chapter. Spectral theory diagonalizes operators into eigenvalues and eigenfunctions and is the analytic core of spectral graph and manifold learning. The deck follows PDF pages 55 through 64 and covers eigendecomposition, the graph Laplacian, the Fourier transform as eigenbasis, and spectral convolution.

label: Eigenvalues and Eigenfunctions
notes: Recall eigenvalues and eigenfunctions and the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators: a complete orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. Diagonalization expresses the operator as scaling along eigen-directions, turning hard operator equations into independent scalar equations that are far easier to solve.

label: The Graph Laplacian
notes: Define the graph Laplacian as degree minus adjacency, and its normalized variants. It is symmetric positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues are non-negative and eigenvectors orthogonal. The Laplacian encodes connectivity and smoothness and is the central operator of spectral graph theory.

label: Fourier as Eigenbasis
notes: Reframe the Fourier transform as the eigenbasis of the Laplacian: classical Fourier modes are Laplacian eigenfunctions on regular domains. On graphs, the Laplacian eigenvectors define the graph Fourier transform, generalizing the notion of frequency to arbitrary irregular structure.

label: Spectral Convolution
notes: Define convolution as multiplication in the spectral domain. A spectral filter scales each Laplacian eigen-component, then transforms back. This is the principle behind spectral graph neural networks; polynomial filters make it local and efficient, avoiding full eigendecomposition.

label: Recap
notes: Close the chapter. Spectral theory diagonalizes self-adjoint operators, the graph Laplacian carries connectivity, its eigenbasis generalizes Fourier analysis, and spectral convolution filters signals by frequency. This completes the analytic toolkit, with graph theory in Chapter 07 supplying the combinatorial side.
